statement: To a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them both medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.
heath_proof: Let AB be the straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, and BC an annex to it; therefore AC, CB are straight lines incommensurable in square which fulfil the aforesaid conditions. [X. 78] I say that no other straight line can be annexed to AB which fulfils the aforesaid conditions. For, if possible, let BD be so annexed, so that AD, DB are also straight lines incommensurable in square which make the squares on AD, DB added together medial, twice the rectangle AD, DB medial, and also the squares on AD, DB incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD, DB. [X. 78] Let a rational straight line EF be set out, let EG equal to the squares on AC, CB be applied to EF, producing EM as breadth, and let HG equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB be applied to EF, producing HM as breadth; therefore the remainder, the square on AB [II. 7], is equal to EL; therefore AB is the “side” of EL. Again, let EI equal to the squares on AD, DB be applied to EF, producing EN as breadth. But the square on AB is also equal to EL; therefore the remainder, twice the rectangle AD, DB [II. 7], is equal to HI. Now, since the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial and is equal to EG, therefore EG is also medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, producing EM as breadth; therefore EM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF. [X. 22] Again, since twice the rectangle AC, CB is medial and is equal to HG, therefore HG is also medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, producing HM as breadth; therefore HM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF. [X. 22] And, since the squares on AC, CB are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB, EG is also incommensurable with HG; therefore EM is also incommensurable in length with MH. [VI. 1, X. 11] And both are rational; therefore EM, MH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EH is an apotome, and HM an annex to it. [X. 73] Similarly we can prove that EH is again an apotome and HN an annex to it. Therefore to an apotome different rational straight lines are annexed which are commensurable with the wholes in square only: which was proved impossible. [X. 79] Therefore no other straight line can be so annexed to AB. Therefore to AB only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole makes the squares on them added together medial, twice the rectangle contained by them medial, and also the squares on them incommensurable with twice the rectangle contained by them.
ai_proof_text:
10.84
**Statement:** To a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them both medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, and let BC be annexed to it, so that AC is incommensurable in square with BC, the sum of the squares on AC and CB is medial, twice the rectangle AC by CB is medial, and the sum of the squares on AC and CB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC by CB [10.78]. I say that no other straight line besides BC can be annexed to AB fulfilling these conditions.

**Step 2.** For, if possible, let BD also be annexed to AB, so that AD is also incommensurable in square with DB, the sum of the squares on AD and DB is medial, twice the rectangle AD by DB is medial, and the sum of the squares on AD and DB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD by DB [10.78].

**Step 3.** Set out a rational straight line EF. Apply to EF the rectangle EG equal to the sum of the squares on AC and CB, producing EM as breadth [1.45]. Subtract from EG the rectangle HG equal to twice the rectangle AC by CB, producing HM as breadth. Then the remainder EH equals the square on AB [2.7], so that EH is the rectangle applied to EF producing EH with breadth equal to the square on AB divided by EF.

**Step 4.** Since the sum of the squares on AC and CB is medial and equals EG, the rectangle EG is medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, so EM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 5.** Since twice the rectangle AC by CB is medial and equals HG, the rectangle HG is also medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, so HM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 6.** Since the sum of the squares on AC and CB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC by CB, the rectangle EG is incommensurable with the rectangle HG. Therefore EM is incommensurable in length with HM [6.1, 10.11].

**Step 7.** Both EM and HM are rational. Therefore EM and HM are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore EH is an apotome [10.73], with HM as its annex.

**Step 8.** Similarly, apply to EF the rectangle EI equal to the sum of the squares on AD and DB, producing EN as breadth. Since the square on AB also equals the remainder when twice the rectangle AD by DB is subtracted from the sum of the squares on AD and DB [2.7], the rectangle EH also equals the square on AB from this decomposition. But EH was also obtained from the first decomposition. Thus EI minus the rectangle equal to twice the rectangle AD by DB equals EG minus HG, that is, they both equal EH.

**Step 9.** Apply to EF the rectangle equal to twice the rectangle AD by DB, and let this equal the rectangle with breadth HN (that is, subtract from EI the rectangle equal to twice the rectangle AD by DB to obtain EH). Then EN is the breadth produced by the sum of the squares on AD and DB applied to EF.

**Step 10.** Since the sum of the squares on AD and DB is medial and equals EI, the rectangle EI is medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, so EN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 11.** Since twice the rectangle AD by DB is medial and is applied to the rational straight line EF producing HN as breadth, HN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 12.** Since the sum of the squares on AD and DB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD by DB, the area EI is incommensurable with the area producing breadth HN. Therefore EN is incommensurable in length with HN [6.1, 10.11].

**Step 13.** Both EN and HN are rational. Therefore EN and HN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore EH is an apotome with HN as its annex [10.73].

**Step 14.** But EH was already shown to be an apotome with HM as its annex [Step 7]. By 10.79, to an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only. Therefore HM equals HN.

**Step 15.** Now, since EG equals the sum of the squares on AC and CB, and EI equals the sum of the squares on AD and DB, and EH equals the square on AB in both cases, the remainder HG equals twice the rectangle AC by CB and the corresponding remainder from EI equals twice the rectangle AD by DB.

**Step 16.** Since the squares on AC and CB equal the squares on AD and DB plus the difference EG minus EI (or vice versa), and twice the rectangle AC by CB and twice the rectangle AD by DB are related correspondingly, we examine the areas. We have EG minus HG equals EI minus the area for twice rect(AD,DB), both equaling EH. Since HM equals HN [Step 14], the areas HG and the rectangle for twice rect(AD,DB) have the same breadth on EF from H, so HG equals twice rect(AD,DB). Therefore EG equals EI, which means the sum of squares on AC, CB equals the sum of squares on AD, DB.

**Step 17.** Since the sum of the squares on AC and CB equals the sum of the squares on AD and DB, and twice the rectangle AC by CB equals twice the rectangle AD by DB, it follows that the square on AC plus the square on CB equals the square on AD plus the square on DB, and the rectangle AC by CB equals the rectangle AD by DB.

**Step 18.** Therefore the square on AC minus the square on AD equals the square on DB minus the square on CB. Also, since AC squared plus CB squared equals AD squared plus DB squared, and these sums are both medial areas equal to one another, and similarly twice rect(AC,CB) equals twice rect(AD,DB), consider the identity: (AC + CB) squared equals the sum of squares on AC, CB plus twice rect(AC,CB), and similarly (AD + DB) squared equals the sum of squares on AD, DB plus twice rect(AD,DB) [2.4]. Since the respective parts are equal, (AC + CB) squared equals (AD + DB) squared, so AC + CB equals AD + DB.

**Step 19.** But also, since AC - CB = AB = AD - DB (both decompositions yield AB as the remainder), we have AC - CB = AD - DB.

**Step 20.** From AC + CB = AD + DB [Step 18] and AC - CB = AD - DB [Step 19], adding these equalities gives 2AC = 2AD, so AC = AD [CN2, CN3]. Subtracting then gives CB = DB, hence BC = BD.

**Step 21.** Therefore to AB, a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, only one straight line BC can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them. Q.E.D.
